articles.title: The Giving Grove: how Kansas City’s free community orchards became a national model
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM It is harvest time in Kansas City, and at Kansas City Academy, students are stepping outside during lunch to pick jujubes straight off the trees. “I feel like a fairy tale princess every lunch,” said Nova Henry, a senior, “because I get to go out and just feast on […]
The post The Giving Grove: how Kansas City’s free community orchards became a national model first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

It is harvest time in Kansas City, and at Kansas City Academy, students are stepping outside during lunch to pick jujubes straight off the trees. “I feel like a fairy tale princess every lunch,” said Nova Henry, a senior, “because I get to go out and just feast on little treats.”

The trees are free for anyone to take from. That is the whole premise of the Giving Grove, a Kansas City organization 14 years into planting fruit orchards on vacant land and asking nothing in return. It now has 14,000 trees in 847 orchards across 17 cities, and more than a million people live within walking distance of one.

The Giving Grove’s origin story

The Giving Grove began with a small stand of trees planted 13 years ago on the corner of a shuttered public school in the Waldo neighborhood. The school has since reopened and is expanding, so the original orchard is currently behind a construction fence, but it is still there. “This little orchard we’re standing in here started a national movement,” said Giving Grove Marketing Director Sarah Sikich. “I think it’s one of Kansas City’s best-kept secrets.”

From that corner, the organization partnered with Kansas City Community Gardens to spread orchards across unused plots throughout the metro, from a few trees on a school parking lot to plots with over a hundred. Kansas City now has 248 free orchards with nearly 4,600 fruit, nut, and berry trees. “I joke that Kansas City should be the city of orchards, not the city of fountains,” Sikich said. “No other city in the United States has as many orchards as we do.”

Built on shared knowledge

More than four out of five Giving Grove orchards remain in production. The reason, according to founder Kevin Birzer, is that the organization never just plants trees and walks away. “It’s stuff people can learn, but it takes a long time, and it’s not really efficient for one group to do that,” he said. “So our thought from day one was we would provide that expertise, the knowledge of how to grow the trees, how to select the trees.”

About 1,700 “orchard stewards” across the country maintain that relationship. The Giving Grove offers training, workshops, help finding grants, soil improvements, pruning support, and succession planning for when stewards move on or burn out. Janet Porter, a science teacher who tends the orchard at Kansas City Academy, has found the same to be true. “They do training. They do workshops. If I ever have any questions, they’re just a phone call away.”

It is not just fruit, either. The trees attract insects, which attract songbirds, which attract predators like hawks. At least one Kansas City student turned pruning experience into a job at a tree nursery.

A model spreading city by city

Nine years ago, a community gardening group in St. Louis asked for help, and the Giving Grove said yes. Now the organization is in cities across the country, with conversations underway about San Francisco, Minneapolis, and New York City.

Different communities want different trees, and growing in Brooklyn is not the same as growing in Utah, especially without chemical pesticides or herbicides. “Some environments are more challenging,” Birzer said. “Creating something really cool for the neighborhood, that part’s universal.”

The Giving Grove runs on just over $1 million a year. Most of it comes from 1% for the Planet, a network that channels one percent of member businesses’ annual revenue toward environmental causes; corporations sometimes add volunteer labor, and individual donors fill in the rest. The organization only enters communities that invite it, and right now it is working through a backlog of those invitations.

“I think people have an easy time falling in love with what we’re doing,” Sikich said. “Planting fruit trees is something everyone can agree with.”

articles.title: One of Earth’s most powerful supervolcanoes is refilling with fresh magma
articles.summary: Deep beneath Japan’s Kikai caldera, a massive magma reservoir is refilling 7,300 years after one of the most powerful volcanic eruptions in Earth's recent geological history. Scientists used underwater seismic surveys to reveal a vast store of magma that appears to have accumulated since the ancient catastrophe. The discovery could help explain how supervolcanoes like Yellowstone and Toba rebuild their magma supplies.
articles.content:
One of Earth's most powerful supervolcanoes is slowly refilling its enormous underground magma reservoir, thousands of years after producing one of the largest volcanic eruptions in recent geological history. Scientists at Kobe University have discovered evidence that fresh magma is accumulating beneath Japan's Kikai caldera, which unleashed a catastrophic eruption about 7,300 years ago.

The discovery offers a rare look at how giant volcanic systems rebuild their magma supplies after massive eruptions. It could also provide important clues about the behavior of other supervolcanoes, including Yellowstone in the United States and Toba in Indonesia, potentially helping scientists improve their ability to recognize warning signs of future eruptions.

How Supervolcanoes Store Enormous Amounts of Magma

Some volcanic eruptions are so immense that they dramatically reshape the landscape. The amount of magma released can be staggering, enough to bury all of New York City's Central Park beneath a layer roughly 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) thick.

When such enormous volumes of magma escape from underground, the rock above the emptied reservoir can collapse, leaving behind a broad, relatively shallow depression known as a caldera. These features are associated with some of the most powerful eruptions in Earth's history.

Famous examples include Yellowstone, Toba, and Japan's Kikai caldera, most of which lies beneath the ocean. Kikai last experienced a giant eruption approximately 7,300 years ago, producing the largest known volcanic eruption of the Holocene, the geological epoch that began roughly 11,700 years ago and continues today.

Although scientists know that giant caldera volcanoes can erupt more than once, they still have an incomplete understanding of how the enormous quantities of magma required for these events accumulate underground. This makes it extremely difficult to anticipate when another major eruption might occur.

"We must understand how such large quantities of magma can accumulate to understand how giant caldera eruptions occur," says Kobe University geophysicist Nobukazu Seama.

Scientists Discover a Massive Magma Reservoir Beneath Japan

Kikai's underwater location might seem like an obstacle to studying the volcano, but it actually gives researchers an important advantage. The surrounding seafloor allows scientists to carry out extensive geological surveys across the volcanic structure.

"The underwater location allows us to implement systematic, large-scale surveys," Seama explains.

To investigate what lies beneath Kikai, researchers from Kobe University collaborated with the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC). They used powerful airgun arrays to generate seismic pulses that traveled through the crust beneath the ocean floor.

Instruments called ocean bottom seismometers recorded how these waves moved through the underground rock. Because seismic waves travel differently through solid rock and regions containing molten material, scientists can analyze their behavior to investigate structures that cannot be observed directly.

The findings, published in Communications Earth & Environment, revealed a substantial region containing a high proportion of magma directly beneath the site of Kikai's massive eruption 7,300 years ago.

By examining the seismic measurements, the team was able to determine the approximate size and shape of the underground reservoir. Its position and extent suggest that it occupies the same magma storage system involved in the ancient eruption.

"Due to its extent and location it is clear that this is in fact the same magma reservoir as in the previous eruption," Seama says.

Fresh Magma Is Recharging the Ancient Supervolcano

Perhaps the most intriguing finding is that the magma currently beneath Kikai does not appear to be simply leftover material from its catastrophic eruption thousands of years ago.

Previous investigations revealed that a new lava dome has been developing near the center of the caldera over approximately the past 3,900 years. A lava dome forms when relatively thick, viscous lava accumulates around a volcanic vent rather than flowing freely across the surrounding landscape.

Chemical analyses also showed that volcanic material from this dome and other more recent activity differs in composition from the material released during Kikai's giant eruption.

That difference provides an important clue. It suggests that the magma now stored beneath the volcano was supplied by new injections of molten rock from deeper within Earth's crust or mantle, rather than remaining unchanged since the previous eruption.

"This means that the magma that is now present in the magma reservoir under the lava dome is likely newly injected magma," summarizes Seama.

Together, the seismic observations and chemical evidence help researchers develop a clearer picture of how a giant volcanic system can gradually rebuild its underground magma supply following a massive eruption.

This replenishment process does not mean that another catastrophic eruption is imminent. Instead, it reveals how a magma reservoir can be recharged over thousands of years, an important process that scientists need to understand before they can reliably assess the long-term behavior of supervolcanoes.

What the Discovery Could Reveal About Yellowstone

The findings could have implications far beyond Japan.

Researchers believe the process identified beneath Kikai may help explain why other enormous caldera systems, including Yellowstone and Toba, also contain large magma reservoirs relatively close to Earth's surface.

"This magma re-injection model is consistent with the existence of large shallow magma reservoirs beneath other giant calderas like Yellowstone and Toba," says Seama.

The proposed model suggests that, following a giant eruption, new magma can gradually enter and replenish an existing underground reservoir. Understanding how this happens could reveal important patterns in the long-term cycles of magma accumulation, volcanic activity, and major eruptions.

Researchers now hope to improve the seismic techniques used at Kikai so they can investigate the movement and storage of magma in greater detail.

"We want to refine the methods that have proved to be so useful in this study to more deeply understand the re-injection processes. Our ultimate goal is to become better able to monitor the crucial indicators of future giant eruptions."

By revealing how fresh magma accumulates beneath a volcano responsible for one of Earth's most extraordinary eruptions, the research brings scientists closer to understanding the processes that eventually make such colossal events possible.

This research was funded by the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) (The Third Earthquake and Volcano Hazards Observation and Research Program (Earthquake and Volcano Hazard Reduction Research)) and the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (grant 20H00199). It was conducted in collaboration with researchers from the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC).

articles.title: Soil mapping aims to boost agricultural production in Kenya
articles.summary: A new Kenyan initiative is helping farmers better understand their soils in a bid to improve crop yields amid intensifying climate shocks.
articles.content:
The Soil Mapping for Resilient Agrifood systems (SoilFER) programme supports farmers to develop reliable soil information that will inform agricultural decisions such as which fertilizer to use and how much.

So far, more than 3,600 soil samples have been collected and mapped across 45 counties, contributing to a digital soil map designed to provide farmers with location-specific information about their land.

Tweet URL

Select farmers also receive training to diagnose and fix soil degradation – earning the title “soil doctor” – who then go on to teach their peers.

SoilFER was launched through a partnership between the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) in Kabete, with financial support from the United States Department of State and Japan.

‘Now we know better’

For Agness Munialo, a farmer from Kakamega county in western Kenya, learning about soil composition and fertility has changed how she thinks about farming.

“Farmers would use excessive chemicals, sometimes even more fertilizers in an attempt to get more yields. Now we know better,” she said.

Ms. Munialo, a trained soil doctor who participated in the SoilFER programme, said the initiative was helping farmers, particularly in rural areas, better understand soil composition, pH levels and fertility.

According to Barrack Okoba, FAO-Kenya’s national coordinator of the programme, making soil information accessible is essential to building resilience in agriculture.

“Part of resilience is to make sure that our information system is available and supporting farmers to build sustainable farm management,” he said.

Through the support of FAO, KALRO has renovated three labs and equipped them with state-of-the-art technology to support analysis of soil samples collected across the country.

The samples are georeferenced, with the findings transmitted directly to farmers’ mobile phones.

Gen Z in agriculture

The initiative is also attracting interest from young people exploring opportunities in agriculture.



Jackline Kioko, a KALRO intern who participated in the launch, said the information shared had given her a better understanding of how soil testing could inform decisions on her family’s farm.

“I'd love to do farming more, now that I have the information that you can actually test your soils to know what nutrients it requires,” she said.

Collaboration and information sharing

Kenya’s Cabinet Secretary for Agriculture, Mutahi Kagwe called for stronger collaboration among agricultural institutions to promote coordinated decision-making, enhance information sharing, and ensure that soil health is integrated into the work of all relevant institutions.

“I want to urge Kenyans that before thinking about what to plant or the fertilizer to use, think about soil testing,” he said.

The event also marked the launch of the Kenya Soil Partnership, the Kenya Soil Laboratory Network and the national rollout of the Global Soil Doctors Programme.

The SoilFER programme is currently being implemented in six other countries: Ghana, Guatemala, Honduras, Mozambique, Tunisia and Zambia.

articles.personality_title_fr: Le Kenya utilise la cartographie des sols pour aider les agriculteurs à mieux cultiver

Le gouvernement encourage tous les agriculteurs à tester leur sol avant de planter. SoilFER s’étend aussi à six autres pays, partageant cette méthode pour aider plus d’agriculteurs à cultiver des récoltes plus solides.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le programme de cartographie des sols du Kenya fournit aux agriculteurs des informations claires et locales ainsi qu’une formation pour mieux cultiver et protéger leurs terres pour l’avenir.
articles.personality_title_es: Kenia usa mapeo de suelos para ayudar a agricultores a cultivar mejor
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los agricultores en Kenia enfrentan problemas por el clima cambiante y la calidad del suelo, lo que dificulta la producción de alimentos. Un nuevo programa llamado SoilFER comenzó para dar a los agricultores mejor información sobre sus suelos.

**Qué pasó** – SoilFER recogió más de 3,600 muestras de suelo en 45 condados de Kenia. Estas muestras se analizaron y mapearon para crear un mapa digital del suelo. Este mapa ayuda a los agricultores a saber exactamente qué necesita su tierra. Algunos agricultores recibieron entrenamiento para ser "doctores de suelo", que revisan la salud del suelo y enseñan a otros cómo solucionarlo. El programa fue lanzado en alianza con la Organización de las Naciones Unidas para la Alimentación y la Agricultura (FAO) y la Organización de Investigación Agrícola y Ganadera de Kenia (KALRO), con apoyo de Estados Unidos y Japón.

**Impacto** – El programa ayuda a los agricultores a usar la cantidad correcta de fertilizantes en vez de adivinar, lo que ahorra dinero y protege la tierra. Por ejemplo, Agness Munialo, una agricultora entrenada como doctora de suelo, ahora sabe cuidar mejor su tierra y enseña a otros. La información del mapa se envía directamente a los teléfonos de los agricultores, facilitando su uso. El programa también atrae a jóvenes interesados en la agricultura, como Jackline Kioko, quien ve la agricultura como una carrera prometedora gracias a este conocimiento.

**Próximo paso** – Kenia ha lanzado nuevos grupos como la Asociación de Suelos de Kenia y la Red de Laboratorios de Suelos para seguir mejorando la salud del suelo. El gobierno anima a todos los agricultores a hacer pruebas de suelo antes de sembrar. SoilFER también se está expandiendo a seis países más, compartiendo esta forma de ayudar a más agricultores a cultivar cosechas más fuertes.

**Resumen en una frase** – El programa de mapeo de suelos en Kenia ofrece a los agricultores información clara y local junto con capacitación para cultivar mejor y proteger sus tierras para el futuro.

articles.title: Project to restore rare native trees with DNA testing
articles.summary: Conservation groups say black poplars are endangered due to felling, land drainage and habitat loss.
articles.content:
A project is aiming to help restore one of the UK's rare native trees across the Thames Valley using DNA testing.

Conservation groups have warned numbers of black poplar trees have fallen due to decades of felling, land drainage and habitat loss.

The Swindon to Oxford: Regenerating the Thames and Tributaries nature recovery programme is working with local conservation groups to regenerate the population along the River Thames and its flood plain.

Catrina Bass, from the Long Mead Foundation in Swindon, is involved in the project and said while the trees were "extraordinary survivors", there were just 50 recorded in Oxfordshire currently.

Describing black poplars as "Lord of the Rings" looking trees with "great gnarled trunks", she said they support other wildlife, including the poplar hornet moth.

The project secured initial funding from West Oxfordshire District Council and the Vale of White Horse Council but is now aiming to raise £20,000 for the work, which involves DNA analysis of existing trees, propagating new cuttings and planting them in suitable sites.

Oxfordshire County Council's Local Nature Recovery Strategy has committed to match fund the fundraiser up to £10,000.

Also involved in the project is the Trust for Oxfordshire's Environment, which works with community groups to fund local environmental projects.

Chief executive Benjamin Heaven Taylor said black poplars play an important role in reducing flood risk, by lining rivers and floodplains, holding water back.

He said the population that remained was "extremely fragmented", adding that it "needs a helping hand to recover".
articles.reasoning: The article describes a conservation project using DNA testing to restore the rare native black poplar tree population in the UK, which has broad environmental benefits including biodiversity support and flood risk reduction. The project involves multiple local organizations and government funding, indicating significant community and ecological impact.
articles.personality_title: DNA testing helps restore rare black poplar trees in the Thames Valley
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Black poplar trees, one of the UK’s rare native tree species, have become endangered because many have been cut down, and their natural habitats have been damaged by land drainage and development.

**What happened** – A new project called Swindon to Oxford: Regenerating the Thames and Tributaries is working to bring back black poplar trees along the River Thames. Using DNA testing, the project identifies existing trees, grows new ones from cuttings, and plants them in good locations. Local groups and councils have started funding the effort, which aims to raise £20,000 to support the work.

**Impact** – The black poplar trees are important because they provide homes for wildlife like the poplar hornet moth and help reduce flooding by holding back water along rivers. Right now, only about 50 black poplars are recorded in Oxfordshire, and they are spread out in small groups. This project helps increase their numbers and protect the environment.

**What’s next step** – The project will continue fundraising with support from Oxfordshire County Council, which will match up to £10,000. With more funds, they will do more DNA tests, grow more trees, and plant them in the best places to help the black poplar population grow stronger.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Using DNA testing, local groups are working together to restore rare black poplar trees, supporting wildlife and reducing flood risks along the Thames.
articles.personality_title_fr: La restauration des peupliers noirs rares dans la vallée de la Tamise grâce aux tests ADN

Des groupes locaux et des conseils financent cette initiative qui vise à récolter 20 000 £.

Actuellement, environ 50 peupliers noirs sont recensés dans l'Oxfordshire, dispersés en petits groupes. Ce projet aide à augmenter leur nombre et à protéger l'environnement.

articles.personality_title_es: La prueba de ADN ayuda a restaurar los raros álamos negros en el valle del Támesis
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los álamos negros, una especie nativa rara en el Reino Unido, están en peligro porque muchos han sido talados y sus hábitats naturales dañados por el drenaje de tierras y el desarrollo.

**Qué pasó** – Un nuevo proyecto llamado Swindon a Oxford: Regenerando el Támesis y sus afluentes trabaja para recuperar los álamos negros a lo largo del río Támesis. Usando pruebas de ADN, el proyecto identifica los árboles existentes, cultiva nuevos a partir de esquejes y los planta en lugares adecuados. Grupos locales y gobiernos están financiando la iniciativa, que busca recaudar £20,000.

**Impacto** – Los álamos negros son importantes porque brindan hogar a animales como la polilla poplar hornet y ayudan a reducir las inundaciones al retener agua a lo largo de los ríos. Actualmente, sólo hay alrededor de 50 álamos negros registrados en Oxfordshire, dispersos en pequeños grupos. Este proyecto ayuda a aumentar su número y proteger el medio ambiente.

**Próximo paso** – El proyecto continuará recaudando fondos con el apoyo del Consejo del Condado de Oxfordshire, que igualará hasta £10,000. Con más fondos, harán más pruebas de ADN, cultivarán más árboles y los plantarán en los mejores lugares para fortalecer la población de álamos negros.

**Resumen en una frase** – Usando pruebas de ADN, grupos locales trabajan juntos para restaurar los raros álamos negros, apoyando la vida silvestre y reduciendo riesgos de inundación a lo largo del Támesis.
